data.title: AI Broke the Old Proof of Learning. Here's Where Education Stands Heading Into 2027
data.description:
Four years after ChatGPT showed up on campus, nobody in education is still asking whether AI belongs in school. They're improvising answers to harder questions. How do you know a student learned something? What is worth learning when a machine can produce the answer? Who gets to decide?

No one has settled any of this. Here's where things stand in six places as 2027 approaches.

1. Testing goes back into the room

For generations, a finished essay counted as proof that learning had happened behind it. Generative AI broke that link.

In Chris Schaffer's biomedical engineering course at Cornell, teaching assistants no longer grade the written problem sets. Each student sits for an oral defense of their answers instead. At NYU's Stern School of Business, Panos Ipeirotis told the AP, "I don't trust written assignments anymore to be the result of actual thinking." His final is oral too, run by an AI voice agent built with ElevenLabs. He calls it fighting fire with fire.

It goes beyond single courses.

Princeton now requires proctors at all in-person exams, the biggest change to an honor code that dates all the way back to 1893. Demand for blue books is surging again at campuses across the country.

Not everyone thinks this is progress.

Berkeley computer scientist Armando Fox calls handwritten exams "a retreat." Oral exams are hard to scale to a 200-person lecture, rough on anxious students, and won't stop AI glasses or earpieces. Still, several of Schaffer's students told the AP they came to prefer the format.

2. What students should learn

Employers and educators are landing in the same place: judgment, adaptability, and working with people.

At a CUNY Graduate Center panel last month, Cornell vice provost Steve Jackson described what employers say they need from graduates in the AI era. You might expect the answer to be AI skills, and a few do make the list, like knowing which tasks to hand off to a machine and catching it when it's wrong. But the top requests are older than any chatbot: people who keep learning and change their minds when the facts change, and people who work well with others. Even asked about AI, employers mostly want what universities have always tried to teach.

Watch: AI and the Future of Education, CUNY Graduate Center, Oct. 14, 2026

Aankit Patel, CUNY's dean for technology, argued that judgment gets built through the slow work AI makes optional, like summarizing a text yourself and deciding what matters. Education, he noted, is notoriously inefficient, and it isn't supposed to be efficient.

That's a pedagogical argument, not a technical one: the inefficiency is the point.

Colby College president David Greene, speaking to ABC News, goes further. Colby gives every student AI access and has spent six years training faculty through its Davis Institute for Artificial Intelligence. He still argues that when most intelligence is artificial, trained human intelligence becomes a scarce resource. He calls this "a golden hour for the liberal arts."

Cornell is testing a version of that idea, redesigning some humanities courses to run like an architecture studio, with long stretches of work done together in the room.

Watch: College president on how AI is impacting education, ABC News

The obvious question is whether that golden hour reaches anyone outside a place like Colby. Greene doesn't really answer it. Neither, yet, does anyone else.

3. The middle, from a school using it now

An interesting approach is at Trinity International Private School in Cyprus, a new school and the first investment of SP Ventures, the firm Sergey Portnov launched after stepping back from day-to-day management of Parimatch. Head of School Dr Vladimir Kuskovski puts teacher preparation at the center of the discussion. His emphasis is on "what to do with it, rather than what not to do with it."

One practical opportunity, in his view, is helping teachers understand where individual students are struggling. A series of checkpoints throughout a term or teaching unit can provide data for AI to analyze, helping teachers identify different learning gaps and adapt their instruction. Drawing on his experience as a language teacher, Kuskovski notes how difficult that work can be: "It's a lot easier to just say the word differentiation rather than actually do it." The benefit depends on teachers knowing which questions to ask and what they want to understand from the assessment results.

He is more cautious about handing over curriculum design. "I wouldn't necessarily use it yet to build the curriculum, but I would use it to inform curriculum building." For a humanities topic, for example, he suggests using AI to find current resources that can support a teacher's planning. He would not yet trust it to create the full scope and sequence of a subject. His approach leaves teachers responsible for deciding how the information should shape teaching.

ELSA, new to Israeli classrooms, applies the same logic, according to a Nov. 19 report in ynet. Through Safe School, which says it operates in about 1,600 schools, the AI platform for English speaking and pronunciation already used in Japanese schools is being brought into Israeli middle schools, adapted for Hebrew and Arabic speakers and aligned to the Education Ministry curriculum. Founder Doron Herman calls English "the leading gateway to tomorrow's world and the high-tech industry," and says the goal is to let students practice "in a supportive, personalized environment without the anxiety of speaking." Chairman Amit Edri puts the shift more broadly: "the classroom as we knew it is changing, the teacher's role is changing, and every student will learn at their own pace with fully personalized instruction."

4. K-12 is pulling back

New York City, the country's largest district, has put a one-year moratorium on student-facing AI from 2-K through 8th grade, with only limited pilots in high schools.

Los Angeles has barred students from using AI on district devices.

Google has made the same move in its own products: Gemini and its other AI tools will stay off for K-12 student accounts until a school administrator turns them on.

The caution reflects a lack of evidence. NPR recently reported that a Stanford review of more than 800 papers found little solid research on how schools should use AI. What research exists suggests well-designed tools do better than general-purpose chatbots. Districts don't even agree on how to measure success. The consultant behind an AI pilot in Dayton, Ohio, told NPR that every attempt to measure it concretely gets him only as far as how students and staff feel about it.

5. The industry builds the tools and funds the training

Earlier this month, Google announced "Guided Learning," a mode in which its AI coaches students through a problem step by step instead of handing over the answer. It is now available worldwide in Google Classroom and is starting as a pilot in Google Search in selected U.S. schools. The same day, Google.org announced more than $9.5 million for five organizations building AI for teachers, including CUNY's Computing Integrated Teacher Education initiative and Teaching Lab.

New York Times reporter Natasha Singer, author of Coding Kids, sees a familiar cycle. In 1912, Thomas Edison predicted motion pictures would replace textbooks. Later came one laptop per child, then personalized learning apps, then coding for every student. Now, she says, some of the same companies are promising one chatbot per child, while preliminary studies show a gap between the promise and the results.

The overlap runs both ways. The CUNY panel where Singer spoke was moderated by Luke Waltzer, who leads two Google.org-funded AI literacy projects. Fellow panelist Aankit Patel led the CUNY teacher-education program now on Google.org's grant list. Neither fact undercuts what they said. It shows how hard it has become to talk about AI in schools without the industry somewhere in the room.

6. The goalpost keeps moving

The technology is changing faster than schools can study it.

At Anthropic, engineers went from merging about 2,500 code changes a day in May 2026 to more than 30,000 in September. Products built on these models change just as quickly. Anthropic's engineers have described a fix they built for one model, which tended to wrap up long tasks too early. Later models stopped doing it, and the fix became unnecessary. In the company's words, the software around a model encodes assumptions about what the model can't do, and those assumptions go stale as models improve.

School research has the same problem. A study run on this year's tutor may say little about next year's. The answer is the one science always gives: test in real classrooms, keep testing, and drop last term's conclusions when they stop holding.

What 2027 looks like

Colby's Greene expects colleges to be in "a pretty funky spot for three or four years" while they work this out. That sounds right. Assessment is moving back into the room. Curricula are shifting toward judgment and away from producing finished work. Schools are pulling back while the evidence catches up. Companies are redesigning their tools and funding the training around them.

Education will adapt. It just won't get to stop adapting.

Whatever schools settle on in 2027 will be tested against the models of 2028, and the question will need asking again: does this version, used this way, help students do their own thinking?

data.title: AI Orchestrators Are the New Air Controllers
data.description:
Woody Holdmere leads forward-deployed engineering at NiCE and builds AI agents inside client operations. CNBC International reports demand for that orchestration work is surging across industries.

His job barely existed two years ago.

Holdmere likened the role to an air controller who keeps tens of thousands of flights apart without flying the planes. Randstad reported postings for AI orchestration and governance roles rose fifteenfold in four years and sit nearly 400% above last year.

An early adopter at Interprefy, a multilingual meeting provider, described the work as async control of multiple agents plus testing, analytics and performance proof.

That control problem is why testing is hard. Holdmere said AI is not always predictable, so guardrails and repeated testing are the most difficult part of deployment.

Separate hiring tracked by AIML Career shows LangGraph orchestration work in Dubai and ML research engineering in the Bay Area, with banks, telecoms and consultancies staffing their own agent teams. Draup reported banking postings that reference agent orchestration jumped over 1700% in 2026, while US pay for agentic roles runs $115,000 to $239,000.

One hiring manager argued process thinking and commercial judgment beat the CV because talent supply is up only about 300% against a 1300% jump in demand. Another voice in the same report said soft skills are the bottleneck, with 61% of customers finding critical thinking harder to hire than technical skill.

Those two views do not resolve. One manager said an orchestrator belongs in a senior band because when an agent speaks, the company speaks, while another argued orchestration will be part of every job.

No one said who owns the failure when one agent hands work to another and the answer is wrong.

data.title: Hinton Is Right About Risk, Wrong About Proof
data.description:
Geoffrey Hinton told TED that AI takeover is only one risk, alongside remote misuse for cyber attacks, engineered viruses and fake videos to corrupt elections, plus chatbot failures and job loss. No local access is needed in his threat model, only access to capable models and agents.

The obvious reading is that the risk hierarchy is now settled and labs should pivot to making models kinder. I do not buy the sequence. The warnings are vivid and the mechanisms are still missing.

Hinton said it would be irresponsible not to warn if wipeout is possible, after the host said Jensen Huang had dismissed talk of a 10% risk of humanity being wiped out as irresponsible in an interview two weeks ago, per TED. Hinton rejected the claim that the risk is zero by 2030 and defended his record, saying he correctly called neural nets over symbolic AI 50 years ago and told 1,000 researchers at NeurIPS in 2009 to buy NVIDIA chips, a call he said Huang did not make until 2012. He owns the failed call that radiologists would be gone by now, which he said was an offhand hospital lecture joke that went viral. What is missing is any agreed probability, and Hinton offers none.

His most honest line is about interpretability. Hinton said after 50 years studying weights he doubts we will ever fully predict why a model gives one answer, because it depends on a trillion weights, and he said models are developing faster than understanding at places like Anthropic. That work, he said, can link an answer to a few training examples but not explain the full process. For that to support a safety case, interpretability would have to improve faster than scale. It has not.

To be fair, he states the industry claim clearly before he attacks it. Many people say systems do not understand what they say, and Hinton said that is crazy because they can answer any question asked. I concede the demos look like understanding. His leap from there to subjective experience is unproven, built on pink elephants seen on LSD as counterfactual world states and a prism thought experiment with a robot arm. His one sentence rule for superintelligence was, "Be nice to people," Hinton said, on the theory that smarter and kinder are orthogonal and the US and China could collaborate on kindness. Separately from TED, he fears a Chernobyl-like AI disaster late this year or next year that could paralyze power and banking, reported by Barlekha Today and not detailed on stage.

If you are building agents, assume remote misuse on day one and prove kindness before you claim scale.

data.title: Anthropic guide sells control, not proof
data.description:
Anthropic published an enterprise guide to securing Claude Code. No prediction venue lists odds or volume on that guide, so there is nothing to reprice and liquidity is absent. I treat that absence as the limit. Not financial advice. Markets move fast.

The obvious reading is the Claude Blog guide hands security teams a full stack to scale agents safely.

I don't buy completeness.

Anthropic frames layered checks and bounded environments as the path to scale, and Deputy CISO Jason Clinton, who owns agentic risk thinking, says leaders should "make agentic risk legible and bounded" while Salesforce reported 79% more merges per developer and 5% fewer incidents after standardizing on Claude Code, according to Anthropic.

To be fair, centrally locked hard-deny rules, sandboxing and exportable telemetry beat honor-system configs, yet Enterprise Frontier Safeguards is still rolling out in phases and a November 2026 Codonomics field report describes the harder shift from having agents write code faster to redesigning work around the AI-Native SDLC Playbook so agents build on prior work across projects.

If you asked me as a founder, I would keep agents on short-lived credentials, locked registries and human approval for high-risk diffs until those phased safeguards actually land.

data.title: AWS says operators cannot touch your EC2 data
data.description:
AWS says its Nitro System gives cloud operators no login path to customer data across every modern EC2 instance. The design blocks even local access by staff with physical servers. That claim now carries a formal proof for the code that keeps tenants apart.

Can the people who run the cloud still read your virtual machine? AWS says no, and it rebuilt the hardware to make that true.

The hypervisor is the software layer that splits one physical server among many customers. EC2 once ran on Xen, which handled CPU scheduling, device emulation and networking on the main processor, the company said. Starting in 2013, AWS moved those jobs to a custom Nitro Card built with Annapurna Labs, a chip startup Amazon acquired in 2015, and launched the stripped down Nitro Hypervisor in 2017.

That split let AWS remove remote login from the hypervisor and measure firmware at every boot, the company said. Nitro Cards are now in their sixth generation with automatic encryption between supported instances. Memory encryption started with Graviton2 and expanded since, while Graviton4 encrypts high speed links to the Nitro Cards, and AWS says the new EC2 T9g instances based on Graviton5 are generally available as low cost burstable instances with best price performance among general purpose EC2 instances.

Formal verification is mathematical proof that a property holds in every system state. Testing cannot cover every case, so AWS moved isolation checks into a small Nitro Isolation Engine written in a limited subset of Rust. Scientists proved four properties with the Isabelle/HOL proof assistant, the company said: confidentiality and integrity, functional correctness, freedom from runtime errors and memory safety, while independent firm NCC Group found no operator access mechanism in a 2023 review.

Hospitals, banks and agencies face audits that ask how tenants stay separate, and they can now point auditors to hardware with no operator path plus math for the isolation check.

data.title: Richpanel will automate 50% of support in 30 days or refund you
data.description:
Richpanel guarantees 50% support automation in 30 days or it refunds the customer.

Amit RG, CEO of Richpanel, said the firm completed approximately 300 deployments in six months as of an October 2026 interview, per OpenAI. He said, "The intelligence is no longer the bottleneck. It’s everything around it." Human agents use 20 or 30 tools, he said, and procedures often were never written down.

Richpanel built Boss AI to write those procedures and define tool calls for frontline, copilot and quality assurance agents, the company said. It uses GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol for that setup work for accuracy, a split described as an efficiency play by Blockchain.News.

The frontline agent runs on GPT-6 Luna and other OpenAI models because it must handle hundreds of thousands of conversations, the company said. Amit RG said, "What matters is a balance of cost and intelligence," measured against low cost outsourced support. He added, "OpenAI models can run these long-context, longer-horizon tasks while still being very cost efficient." He said AI beat human agents on customer satisfaction in each case.

OpenAI published no baseline ticket mix, retention after day 30, or independent CSAT scores to check that satisfaction claim. A cohort breakdown by volume and ticket type would change the read. Will the 50% hold when the next 300 customers bring messier systems?

data.title: Nvidia Faces S&P Downgrade on Governance
data.description:
The Tech Report host Isaac pressed David Gerard on S&P Global Ratings placing Nvidia on watch for a credit downgrade.

Gerard, author and host of Pivot to AI who tracks AI finance, argued Nvidia governance is impaired because Trump forced Jensen Huang back.

Gerard said Trump called into the Nvidia board meeting on Sunday to guarantee no security problem and even discussed pardoning Huang.

Credit judges whether Nvidia can repay debt while stock only bets price will rise, Gerard said.

Bloomberg reported S&P is weighing a one notch cut after Huang left and returned, a detail Gerard tied to key man risk.

Gerard said Nvidia shares rose for one day after Huang returned then fell again as Oracle slipped toward junk.

Lenders still ask if Nvidia can service debt even when traders bid shares higher, Gerard warned.

data.title: iFood turned 15,000 repos into API calls
data.description:
OpenAI says iFood now fixes code by API call and gets back a merge request. The Remote Agents Platform covers more than 15,000 repositories, according to the company.

Stop watching the bot work.

Each run clones the repo, loads skills, cuts a branch, runs GPT-5.6 Luna in an isolated Ubuntu sandbox, then ships artifacts and a merge request, with more than 25,000 runs completed at US$0.04 per run according to iFood. "Solving this for one repository is easy. The challenge is solving it at scale," says Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer at iFood, who says teams keep business logic and hand off execution.

Security took it first. Its scanner hunts vulnerable dependencies across those repos, and iFood says fixes more than doubled after the move, with Structured Outputs forcing each session into a pass or fail contract.

iFood says it copied the OpenAI Agents API and Batch API for async design. That lineage tracks, since OpenAI launched the Responses API and open-source Agents SDK together in March 2025, with Responses as a superset of Chat Completions, per eesel AI.

You still do not watch dependency bumps in a meeting. You still own the judgment calls the contract cannot grade, and at four cents a run the constraint shifts from headcount to which chores you trust.

data.title: Google AI Answers Cost French Sites 24% of Clicks
data.description:
Did Google's AI answers really erase a quarter of search clicks in France? Ahrefs says yes, with a net 24.4% click-through rate loss three months after launch.

The control group proves it is not seasonal.

An AI Overview is the AI-written answer Google places above classic results to answer the query directly. Google rolled it out in France, according to Ahrefs. Coverage jumped from 0% of tracked keywords in June to 88.5% by November 25, with a 35.4 point jump in August alone, according to Ahrefs.

Ahrefs compared 31,612 French keywords between June and October 2026, per its methodology. Ahrefs found keywords that gained an AI Overview fell from 2.53% CTR to 1.964%, a 22.4% drop, while keywords without one rose 2.6%. Had affected keywords followed that trend they would have hit 2.596%, so observed versus expected is a 24.4% net loss, according to Ahrefs.

No rank is safe. Ahrefs says every position lost more than 20% CTR from June to September 2026, with position one falling from 11.06% to 8.69%. Against a control that rose to 11.78%, the net loss at position one is 26.2%, not 21.4%, according to Ahrefs.

So does intent save commercial pages? Not really. Ahrefs reports informational and navigational queries lost about 25% net CTR and commercial and transactional queries lost about 20%. That early August signal still holds, when 963 domains lost 3.4% CTR in nine days overall and 82.2% of highly exposed domains lost clicks, per Keywords Everywhere citing Ahrefs data scientist Xibeijia Guan.

Intent softens the hit by four to five points.

France gives planners a 25% rule

That leaves the SEO lead with new math. Find AI Overview queries in Ahrefs Site Explorer with the SERP features filter, then apply a 25% CTR cut to their traffic share, as Ahrefs advises. If 40% of traffic comes from those queries, expect about a 10% sitewide loss at constant impressions, so watch that share weekly as coverage spreads.
